get.description:
Everything an actor effectively holds, attributed to its source.

One entry per *(authority, pattern)* pair rather than a deduplicated set:
an actor commonly holds the same pattern through a role bundle **and** a
direct grant, and collapsing them would destroy the answer to "what actually
changes if I revoke this?".

``revocable_by_caller`` is resolved here because it depends on the caller,
not on the entry. It is computed with the same ``covers_any`` the service's
no-escalation check uses, so the control a UI offers and the refusal the
service would issue cannot disagree — but it is **advisory**: revocation
still goes through ``AuthzGrantService``, which re-runs the check.

schema.title: Response List Effective Permissions V1 Orgs  Org Id  Permissions Get

get.description:
Everything that *can* be granted — not merely what somebody holds.

The other reads on this router describe a holder, so none of them can name a
permission nobody has yet, and a UI built on them can only ever render
authority that already exists. This is the endpoint that lets one show the
whole grantable set and mark which entries are enabled.

**Two sources, unioned**: the permissions the API's own route gates name, and
the requirements in ``tool_catalog_permissions``. Either alone omits real
permissions — the tool side cannot see the human-only surface
(``platform:*``, ``member:invitation.*``, ``authz:permission.*``), and the
route side cannot see a tool requirement no endpoint gates. Role bundles are
deliberately *not* a third source: they are pattern-valued, hold almost no
fully-concrete patterns, and a ``None`` axis cannot be expanded without the
very universe this endpoint builds. They serve instead as its completeness
oracle, asserted in the tests.

**Wildcards are entries, not something the caller expands.** Every wildcard
shape carries its own ``id``, so a held grant maps to exactly one entry
whatever its shape and ``audit:*.*`` ticks the domain-scope entry rather than
fanning out over the six audit leaves. That matters because expanding it
would report "6 of 6", when the grant actually covers every audit permission
*including ones that do not exist yet* — under-reporting reach, which is the
dangerous direction here. See ``covers_uncatalogued``.

The catalogue is platform vocabulary rather than org data, so the response
does not vary by ``org_id``; the route is org-scoped because it is called
from an org's permissions UI, and org-scoping is what keeps the
org-membership check and org MFA in the chain.

Read-only, and decides nothing: it never consults an actor, grant, or role
assignment.

**It lists what the platform *enforces*, which is narrower than what the
grant API will accept — so a consumer must render this catalogue UNION the
actor's held permissions, never the catalogue alone.**
``AuthzGrantService.grant`` checks only that the granter's own patterns
cover the requested one; it never consults this catalogue. An org owner
holding ``org:*.*`` can therefore write an inert but valid pattern such as
``org:fleet.merge``, which no route gates and no tool requires, and the
actor will hold a row with no entry here. Rendering the catalogue alone
would silently drop that grant — the very failure this endpoint exists to
fix, reintroduced one layer up. See ``is_exhaustive``.

Gated on the same ``authz:permission.read`` that gates reading who holds
what — the grantable vocabulary and the current assignments are the two
halves of one view, and splitting their gates would let a caller see one
without the other for no security benefit.

Who holds a permission — by direct grant, by role, and by self grant.

All three paths, because a lookup covering only some of them reports a
subset as though it were the whole set, and "no holders" reads as a finding
rather than as a gap.

Every holder carries its ``scope`` and its ``scope_shape``, and callers must
render the **three** shapes distinguishably: authority over every instance of
the kind, over one named record, or over everything belonging to one named
record. The same permission triple can name any of them, and merging them
reports the holder of a narrow grant as holding broad authority over every
instance.

Group by permission **and** shape, then name the members inside; never group
across shapes. ``anchored`` is part of the vocabulary from today even though
nothing emits it until anchored scope ships, so a client written against this
payload now needs no change when it starts appearing.

Takes a **concrete** permission, so all three axes are required: this
answers "who can do this specific thing" (``matches`` semantics). Wildcard
grants are still found — a ``secret:*`` row genuinely confers
``secret:secret.create`` and appears here.

schema.title: Response List Permission Holders V1 Orgs  Org Id  Permission Holders Get

get.description:
Which assigned tools would stop working if this grant were revoked.

Feeds the confirm step of a revoke. **Impact is a difference, not a pattern
match**: a tool counts only if it is assigned, works now, and would not work
after the removal. A tool still covered by another grant or by the role floor
is unaffected and is not counted — an over-reporting confirmation is worse
than none, because it teaches people to click through the dialog that exists
to stop them.

Read-only. Revoking still goes through ``AuthzGrantService``; this endpoint
cannot remove anything, and re-granting re-adds no tools because the grant
path never touches assignment.

Which tools a role-bundle change would disable, **across the whole org**.

The wide case, and the reason a preview exists at all. The bot-carried role
keys have no assignment table — every bot in the org holds them
unconditionally — so deleting one ``role_permissions`` row can strip tools
fleet-wide from a single click. ``bot_count`` and ``tool_count`` are served
so the warning can be specific (*"removes 37 tools across 9 bots"*) rather
than vague, and so the headline cannot disagree with the detail beneath it.

post.description:
Grant one permission pattern to one actor in this organization.

Holding ``authz:permission.create`` is necessary but **not sufficient**: the
service additionally refuses to grant any pattern the granter does not hold
itself (403), refuses to write into another organization (403), and refuses
``platform:team.manage`` to a non-human (403). Those refusals are raised by
the service and surfaced by the registered exception handlers — this route
does not re-check, re-word, or catch them.

delete.description:
Revoke a direct grant by id.

A grant id is a **global** handle, so the route's org prefix is not what
contains this: the service re-derives the row's own organization and applies
tenant containment plus authority over the pattern being removed. Without
that, any caller reaching this endpoint could strip authority from an actor
in another organization. Revocation removes authority rather than adding it,
so it cannot escalate — but it is emphatically not unauthenticated, and it is
audited with the same weight as a grant.

post.description:
Create a new bot with the same definition as an existing one.

Copies what the source bot *is*: its config, managed workspace files,
skills, tools, tool domain settings, credential assignments, and
(by default) its Runtime Vault policy links. Does not copy what it has
*lived* — memory, conversations, disk, schedules, devices, health, its
email address, or its access list. The caller becomes the copy's owner.

Two gates apply. ``bot:bot.create`` because this creates a bot, and so the
copy is metered and capped exactly like any other creation
(``MeterKey.BOT_COUNT``); and bot ownership of the *source*, because
copying reads its whole definition — including which secrets it can reach.

Search bots using a JSON filter DSL (recursive AND/OR/Condition).

An empty body (or one with only ``pagination``) is equivalent to
``GET /bots``. See ``core/src/botyard_core/filters/AGENTS.md`` for the
wire-format spec and ``BotFilterField`` for the list of filterable fields.

List the ``(hosting_type, harness)`` combinations a bot may be created with.

patch.description:
Update bot metadata, compute overrides, or runtime privilege mode.

Tier, resource-override, and runtime privilege changes trigger a full K8s
reconcile. Avatar changes are metadata-only. For config changes, use PATCH
/{bot_slug}/config.

Per-bot resource overrides are available on every plan (bounded by the
plan's ``resource_maximums``). Privileged runtime mode is still gated to
plans with the ``privileged_mode`` feature; plans without it receive 403
``upgrade_required``.

get.description:
Lightweight readiness signals for chat surfaces (widget/console).

Cheap, pollable signal: ``llm_configured`` lets a surface warn — before any
send — that the bot can't respond until a credential is assigned, and
``maintenance_restart_pending`` drives a subtle "restart pending" indicator
while a workload-aware maintenance restart is in flight. Visibility-gated
exactly like ``get_bot`` so restricted bots stay 404-invisible to actors
without access.
Get live runtime storage, memory, and CPU usage for a bot.

post.description:
Restart a bot runtime container by deleting its pod.

This mirrors the operator/k9s recovery action: the provisioner deletes the
current pod and the deployment recreates it. Visibility alone is not enough
for this mutating runtime action — org owners/platform admins may restart
any visible bot, and regular users must have bot use access.

patch.description:
Update bot config: persist, return, and trigger reconcile in the background.

Validation is synchronous — an invalid patch, or a config incompatible with
the bot's pinned OpenClaw version, still fails here with a 422. The bridge
*push* is not: the config is persisted with a bumped ``config_generation``
and the provisioner's config reconciler delivers it.

That split is deliberate. A bridge config apply restarts the bot's OpenClaw
process (see ``patch_and_persist_async``), so the previous push-first
behaviour made every individual settings edit cost a full restart inside the
request. Deferring lets the UI stage a batch of edits and converge them in
one restart. Callers that need the bridge's runtime verdict inline use
``patch_and_push`` instead.

Deferring the push is **not** the same as waiting for the next sweep, and the
difference is the whole user-visible latency of a settings change. Like the
skill and tool assignment routes (``bot_skills._commit_and_notify``), we
commit and then nudge the provisioner immediately, in the background: the
response is not held open for the reconcile, but reconciliation starts now
rather than whenever the reconciler next happens to look. The sweep remains
the fallback if the trigger fails, so this is a latency optimisation and not
a correctness dependency.

Only a real change is notified. ``patch_and_persist_async`` returns ``None``
for a value-preserving patch, which bumps no generation — triggering a
reconcile for it would ask the provisioner to converge state that already
matches.

post.description:
End a guided-setup bot's onboarding (the user-facing "skip setup" action).

The human equivalent of the bot-driven ``finish_onboarding`` MCP tool: flips
``onboarding_state`` pending -> complete so the chat service stops injecting
the onboarding directive, and unassigns the onboarding-only skill + tool.
Idempotent — a no-op when the bot is not pending.

Set desired_state=suspended and enqueue reconcile notification.

Gated on bot ownership, matching ``delete_bot`` rather than the looser
can-use ladder of ``restart_bot``: restarting a bot is a recovery action
that returns it to the state its users expect, while suspending it takes
the bot away from every one of them until an owner brings it back.

Idempotent — suspending an already-suspended bot returns the bot unchanged
and skips the provisioner notification.

Set desired_state=running for a suspended bot and enqueue reconcile.

A bot that is not suspended is returned unchanged: resume is the inverse of
suspend, not a general "force this bot back to running" lever.

post.description:
Revoke devices. *** THE BOT IS NOT TOUCHED. ***

This is the stolen-laptop path. Revoking denies the device on its next
assertion exchange and leaves the bot, its conversations, its memory and
its task history entirely intact — which is why revocation targets a
device and not a bot.

Idempotent: revoking an already-revoked device is a no-op that leaves the
original ``revoked_at`` in place, and is still audited, because a repeated
revoke attempt is itself worth seeing.

Force a ``tools/list`` re-handshake by bumping ``config_generation``.

post.description:
Re-enter the reconciler queue for a FAILED MCP server.

Resets the row to ``observed_state=pending``, clears ``last_error`` and
any stuck operator lease, and bumps ``config_generation`` so the
provisioner treats it as drift-to-apply on the next sweep. Returns
``409 Conflict`` when the row is not currently FAILED — re-entering a
healthy or in-flight row would fight the reconciler's own lease and
leak confusing errors back to the operator.

post.summary: List currently streaming conversations visible to the caller
post.description:
Return active streaming turns visible to the caller.

Workforce boards, chat surfaces, and other aggregate views need a
cold-start snapshot of which conversations are currently streaming. The
chat message list exposes this per conversation; this bulk endpoint applies
the same lease TTL and conversation visibility rules.

With ``all_visible=True`` the caller gets every active turn it can see and
filters locally — preferred for the chat polls, which watch an unbounded
number of conversations but only ever see a small set of live streams.
Otherwise the result is narrowed to the requested ``conversation_ids``
and/or ``bot_slugs`` (OR-combined).

Authorization is layered: ``conversation:content_block.read`` names the
capability (and brings org membership + org MFA with it), while
``require_conversation_access`` confines the read to a conversation this
viewer can actually see. The sibling payload/task routes enforce only the
latter because they predate the named-permission migration.

The URL is **minted per request** rather than persisted on the block. A
presigned URL stored in tool-return metadata would go stale — the message read
path re-signs user-prompt parts and the ``media`` column, not tool returns — so
a block that carried its own URLs would rot into dead links. The filename,
content type, and size come from object metadata rather than the request, so a

get.summary: Read a board-task content block's current (live) state
get.description:
Return a board-task content block's **current** renderable state.

The durable ``task`` block carries only a reference (``workforce_slug`` +
``task_number``); this endpoint resolves the task's protected content on
demand so the renderer can draw the live card. Because the content lives only
here — behind the membership gate — and never in the conversation payload, a
conversation-reader who isn't a board member cannot obtain it.

Authorization is layered:

- ``require_conversation_access`` confines the read to a conversation the
  viewer can see — the same surface guard as the sibling payload route.
- **Workforce membership** is the task's own read-access rule (the VIEW
  claim ``get_task`` / ``get_workforce`` enforce). A viewer with
  conversation access but no board access gets ``403`` — the renderer maps
  that to a "no access / unavailable" card, exactly like a linked
  conversation the viewer can't see. A missing/deleted task or board is
  ``404``.

The state shares the reference fields with the inline block (both via
``botyard_core.services.api.task_block``), so the card resolves crumb,
deeplink, and content from this single fetch.

patch.description:
Save this respondent's draft answers, enforcing the per-field revision check.

Called on every debounced edit, so it is deliberately cheap and partial: it
stores drafts, never submits, and never wakes the bot. A stale
``expected_revision`` returns 409 naming the field to re-read.

post.description:
Finalize this respondent's answers and wake the bot once with them.

Saves any answers carried in the body, checks every required field is
answered, marks this respondent's answers final under a row lock (one-shot per
person, not per question), and schedules a single post-commit wake naming the
respondent. Other respondents' drafts are untouched and the question stays
open — closing it is the bot's decision, because only the bot knows how many
answers it needed.

get.description: Return the live status of a vault input request group (never any value).

post.description:
Store the user-supplied secret value(s) for a request group and wake the bot.

Locks the whole pending group (one-shot), re-checks conflicts at each (possibly
user-edited) key, then for every secret either creates a new bot-owned secret or
— when the secret opted into ``allow_update`` and the requesting bot is already
authorized for the existing key — replaces just that key's value, all in one
transaction; marks the group submitted; and schedules a single post-commit wake.
Submission is **all-or-nothing** and must cover exactly the secrets in the group;
the values are never logged or echoed back.

Any user with conversation access may fulfill the request for the requesting
bot. **Broadening** the secrets to other bots or all bots is a cross-bot
distribution decision — owner-gated exactly like the normal secret modal — so
``bot_ids``/``allow_all_bots`` require org-owner role. The pending request only
authorizes storing the secrets for the bot that asked.

Send a chat message; bot response arrives over Centrifugo.

``mode=steer`` injects the message into the active turn instead of queueing
it behind one (no-op if no turn is active). Default ``queue`` preserves the
prior ordering behaviour.

Wake an idle conversation with a hidden developer message.

Starts a bot turn carrying the message as system context — invisible in
the chat UI but read by the bot's model. Intended for automations
(webhooks, schedulers, polling processes) that need to nudge a bot
without keeping a session open. If the conversation already has a
running or queued turn, nothing is sent and status is 'already_active'.

Promote an already-queued message to steer.

Forwards a steer signal to the bot, which pulls the queued message out of
its ordering gate and injects it into the active turn. Whether the message
is still queued (vs. already dispatched) is decided by the bot, which
no-ops if the steer arrived too late.

``require_conversation`` enforces access and hands us the row, so we reuse
its ``bot_id`` instead of re-fetching the conversation.

Cancel an already-queued message before it runs.

Forwards a cancel signal to the bot, which pulls the queued message out of
its ordering gate and drops it so it never runs (the proxy then marks the
turn ``cancelled``). Whether the message is still queued (vs. already
dispatched) is decided by the bot, which no-ops if the cancel arrived too
late.

``require_conversation`` enforces access and hands us the row, so we reuse
its ``bot_id`` instead of re-fetching the conversation.

Edit an already-queued message's content (text and/or attachments).

Locates the queued turn by ``request_id`` and rewrites its content in place —
the bot swaps the queued payload in its ordering gate so the new content is
what dispatches, and the persisted row is updated so the transcript matches.
Returns 409 when the message is no longer queued (already dispatched or
dismissed) or the bot has no live connection; the edit is a safe no-op in
that case.

Exchange a signed device assertion for a short-lived runtime session.

The device registry is read live on every call and a device that is not
active is refused here, before its signature is even examined. There is no
cache, no TTL and no memoised lookup between that row and this decision,
and there must never be one: it is the only reason a credential that never
expires can still be revoked.

Redeem an enrollment token, registering this machine as the bot's device.

Registering the public key and consuming the token are atomic: the token
is spent by a conditional UPDATE that exactly one concurrent caller can
win, and the device row is written in the same transaction, so a token is
never consumed without producing the device it paid for.

No session, assertion or SVID is issued here. The device credential buys
only the right to *ask* for one, on every future connection, against a
registry that can deny it immediately.

*** THERE IS EXACTLY ONE WAY TO LEAVE HERE WITHOUT A DEVICE ROW, AND IT IS
AN ERROR. *** A 2xx from this endpoint means the registry holds a live,
active device for the caller — either written by this call (``201``,
``newly_enrolled``) or read back within it (``200``, the machine already
being that device and offering its key). The caller may therefore treat
"this call succeeded" as "a device exists server-side", which is the
property an installer needs and the one it cannot establish for itself.

get.description:
Active task counts per column, for every board in the org the caller may view.

Exists because there was no way to answer "how are this board's tasks
distributed across its columns" without listing the tasks themselves. The
task list caps ``limit`` at 100, so the largest board in production (2002
tasks, 6.6 MB of title and description text) needs 21 pages to be counted
client-side; asking per column instead trades that for one request per
(board, column), which on the same org is 53 requests. Both are worse than
a single indexed aggregate, which is what this is.

The collision with ``/{workforce_slug}`` is guarded twice, and the order
matters. **First**, ``RESERVED_WORKFORCE_SLUGS`` refuses this slug on
create and on update, so no board can newly reach it — relying on route
order alone would let an authorised editor create a board that is then
reachable at neither its detail GET nor its PATCH, which is worse than the
ambiguity it avoids. **Second**, this route is still registered ahead of
``/{workforce_slug}`` so the aggregate wins for legacy rows and for values
written straight to the database, which the service layer never sees. That
ordering is the same trade ``/tasks/tags`` already makes against
``/tasks/{task_id}``; the difference is that here it is the fallback rather
than the only defence.

post.description: Create a schedule (fire-and-forget).

Explain a candidate spec as concrete upcoming instants. Persists nothing.

Exists because a cron expression is unreadable: the edit dialog needs to
show *when this will actually fire* for a spec the user is still typing, and
a saved schedule's ``next_fire_at`` can only answer that for one occurrence
of an already-saved row.

Answering server-side is a deliberate choice over parsing cron in the
browser. This shares :func:`compute_next_fire_ats` — and therefore
``croniter`` and ``ZoneInfo`` — with the ``next_fire_at`` every read already
derives, so the preview cannot disagree with the schedule it is previewing.
A second, client-side implementation would have to re-solve DST, and would
be wrong twice a year in a way nothing here would catch.

An unparseable spec is a 4xx (the same ``SpecValidationError`` mapping the
write paths use), which lets a half-typed cron expression be reported as
invalid rather than as "no upcoming runs".

platform database. Tenancy is therefore enforced here, before that cluster is
touched: the schedule is first resolved under this org+bot via the platform
database, so an id belonging to another tenant 404s rather than reaching the
history query. If scheduler-postgres is unavailable this returns 503
``schedule_history_unavailable`` — schedules CRUD is unaffected.

action, so it pushes synchronously in the request path and returns the
resulting per-skill deploy status directly.

post.description:
Which permissions this tool set requires, and which the bot lacks.

**One call for the whole set.** Beyond the obvious cost saving over N calls,
a single resolution makes the answer internally consistent: N calls could
interleave with a concurrent grant and return a combination of statuses that
no single moment ever produced, which a user would then act on as a snapshot.

A ``POST`` because the tool-id set is a request body, not because it writes.
**Nothing here grants, revokes or assigns anything** — it reports. Issuance
stays in ``AuthzGrantService`` with its no-escalation, tenant-containment and
audit guarantees, and ``grantable_by_caller`` is advisory: the service
re-runs the identical ``covers`` check on the write, so a client that ignores
this answer gains nothing.

Gated on reading the bot's tools rather than on ``authz:permission.read``:
the question is *"what do these tools need?"*, asked by whoever is looking at
the tool picker. It discloses the bot's authority only as a per-requirement
satisfied/missing flag, which is strictly less than the permissions surface
already returns to a holder of that permission.

AdminActionPerformedContent.title: AdminActionPerformedContent
AdminActionPerformedContent.description:
Typed content for a privileged ``/v1/admin`` mutation.

The **security-attribution floor** for the admin surface: emitted by the
authorization enforcement point itself whenever a mutating platform
permission is granted, so a route is audited *by virtue of being gated*
rather than by someone remembering to add a builder. That structural
property is what the interim bot-write guard's removal rests on — a
per-operation builder is something a future route can forget, and a
guarantee that depends on nobody forgetting is not a guarantee.

It records the *authorization* of the action, since the enforcement point
runs before the handler: "this principal was permitted to perform this
operation". Richer, semantically-typed events (``rollout.initiated``,
``provisioning.maintenance_restart.force_applied``,
``admin.platform_team.*``) remain the record of what the operation actually
did, and are deliberately **not** suppressed by this one — the two answer
different questions, and suppression logic is precisely what would let the
floor develop holes.

``permission`` is the canonical ``domain:resource.action`` id;
``route`` is the path *template* (never the resolved path, so ids do not
leak into the event type's shape); ``path_params`` carries the resolved
path parameters, which is what identifies the affected object.

BotDeviceAssertionDeniedContent.title: BotDeviceAssertionDeniedContent
BotDeviceAssertionDeniedContent.description:
Typed content for a refused assertion exchange or session use.

``reason`` is the granular denial, which the *caller* is never told — the
API answers every refusal identically so the endpoint cannot be used as an
oracle for the registry's contents. The trail is where the distinction is
kept, because a human reading it later has context the endpoint does not.

``device_revoked`` is the reason worth alerting on: it means somebody is
still presenting the credential of a machine that was revoked, which is
the stolen-laptop signal.

BotDeviceCustodyTier.title: BotDeviceCustodyTier
BotDeviceCustodyTier.description:
Where a device *claims* to keep its private key.

*** SELF-DECLARED AND NON-SECURITY-BEARING. NEVER AN AUTHORIZATION
INPUT. ***

Useful for UX, inventory, support and org-level telemetry. Any
authorization that branches on this field is a **spoofable authorization
decision**, because the value is whatever the enrolling client said it
was. UI must render it as "reported by device", never as "verified".

The reasoning, which is the part that must survive:

* **macOS custody is definitively unattestable.** There is no public API
  to attest an arbitrary Secure Enclave key, and App Attest needs an
  App-Store-shaped bundle identity that a ``curl | sh`` CLI will never
  have.
* Windows and Linux with a TPM genuinely *can* prove custody — **and it
  does not help.** A tier ladder is only as attestable as its weakest
  rung: a client wishing to overstate its custody simply reports macOS +
  hardware, which we have nothing to check against. Attesting two of
  three platforms would not make the field trustworthy, it would make it
  *look* trustworthy, which is worse.
* Even complete attestation proves "this key lives in a genuine TPM",
  never "this host is not compromised".

A minimum-tier org policy is therefore an honour system, and must be sold
as one. The real control is that every use is server-mediated and
revocation is an immediate server-side deny checked on every assertion
exchange.

BotDeviceEffectCoverage.title: BotDeviceEffectCoverage
BotDeviceEffectCoverage.description:
How much of what a runtime does is actually mediated by Botyard.

Declared by the runtime and recorded per device. It exists so that a
clean effect ledger is never later misread as proof that nothing
happened.

A v0 external bot declares :attr:`PARTIAL`, and the reason is concrete:
the user's own Claude Code edits files and runs ``git push`` with zero
daemon involvement, so the platform observes a strict subset of that
bot's effects.

BotDeviceEnrolledContent.title: BotDeviceEnrolledContent
BotDeviceEnrolledContent.description:
Typed content for a device completing enrollment.

``custody_tier`` is recorded because it is useful for inventory and
support — **not** because it was checked. It is self-declared and carries
no security weight; see :class:`~botyard_core.models.enums.BotDeviceCustodyTier`.

BotDeviceEnrollmentTokenMintedContent.title: BotDeviceEnrollmentTokenMintedContent
BotDeviceEnrollmentTokenMintedContent.description:
Typed content for minting or regenerating an enrollment token.

``regenerated`` distinguishes the first mint from a replacement, and
``invalidated_token_count`` records how many previously live tokens the
mint killed — regeneration invalidates the prior token immediately, and
the audit trail should show that it happened rather than leaving a reader
to assume it.

The plaintext token appears nowhere in this content, for the same reason
it appears nowhere in the database.

BotDeviceEnrollmentTokenReplayedContent.title: BotDeviceEnrollmentTokenReplayedContent
BotDeviceEnrollmentTokenReplayedContent.description:
Typed content for a redemption attempt against a non-live token.

*** THIS IS THE SECURITY EVENT, AND ITS WHOLE POINT IS THAT WE CANNOT
TELL THE TWO CAUSES APART. *** Either the legitimate user re-ran the
installer, or somebody else is holding a token they should not have. No
field here resolves that ambiguity and none can — the event exists so a
human reading the trail can, with context we do not have.

``reason`` says *how* the token failed to be live, which is the part we do
know. ``presented_public_key`` is recorded because a replay presenting a
**different** key than the enrolled device is the strong signal: a user
re-running an installer normally presents the key they already have.

``devices`` is the post-revocation state of each requested device. The bot

touch it — the bot, its conversations and its history are unaffected.

BotDeviceRevokedContent.title: BotDeviceRevokedContent
BotDeviceRevokedContent.description:
Typed content for revoking a device.

Deliberately records that the bot survives: revocation targets a device,
and the bot, its conversations and its history are untouched.

BotDeviceStatus.title: BotDeviceStatus
BotDeviceStatus.description:
Lifecycle of one enrolled device.

Deliberately only two members. A device row comes into existence *at
redemption* — the row and its registered public key are written in the
same transaction that consumes the enrollment token — so a device is
``ACTIVE`` from the instant it exists. There is no moment at which a
device row is "pending".

What people mean by "pending" belongs to the **bot**, not the device: a
``self_hosted`` bot with a live enrollment token and no device row is
awaiting enrollment. That is *derived* from the absence of a device, not
stored on one, which is why no ``PENDING`` member exists here. A label no
code path can produce is read by every later maintainer as meaningful
state; adding a member later is one ``ALTER TYPE``, un-teaching a
misunderstood one is not.

BotEmailSentContent.title: BotEmailSentContent
BotEmailSentContent.description:
Typed content for a bot sending a single outbound email via Resend.

Emitted once per successful ``send_email`` MCP tool call. The enforced
``from_address`` is derived server-side from the bot/org identity — the
caller never supplies it — so it is recorded here for traceability.
Recipient addresses and the subject are retained for abuse investigation;
the email body is intentionally never stored. ``message_id`` is the Resend
message identifier returned by the provider.

more interesting record: it names a command a bot tried to run in its own
container and the reason the runtime would not run it.

``command`` is the shell string the bridge was asked to spawn, truncated but
never summarised — an audit trail that records "a command was run" without
recording which one answers no question anybody asks. It is absent for a
``pid`` attach, where there is no command to record and ``target_pid`` is

BotRuntimeToolCalledContent.title: BotRuntimeToolCalledContent
BotRuntimeToolCalledContent.description:
Typed content for any MCP tool call observed by the audit middleware.

Covers both first-party platform tools and external/BYO MCP tools.

``args_json`` / ``output_json`` hold the serialized tool arguments and result.
Both are ``None`` when the secrets scanner flagged a leased secret in the call
(all-or-nothing redaction — botyard-mcp never holds plaintext secrets to redact
in place) or when the scan could not run. Large outputs are head+tail truncated
(``output_truncated``); ``output_bytes`` always records the full, uncapped size.

BotRuntimeTrustTier.title: BotRuntimeTrustTier
BotRuntimeTrustTier.description:
The deployment shape a runtime was enrolled under.

*** NON-SECURITY-BEARING. NEVER AN AUTHORIZATION INPUT. ***

Recorded so credential eligibility, provider egress and support posture
have a seam to hang off later, and so a reader can tell what kind of host
a bot runs on without a live connection. It is emphatically **not** a
weaker platform principal: an external bot is a bot, and the tools it
calls execute in-cluster where the ordinary principal/permission model
already governs the decision. Branching platform-tool authorization on
this field would re-decide that, in the wrong place and by accident.

Only one member exists, and that is deliberate rather than an oversight —
the same reasoning that kept ``PENDING`` off :class:`BotDeviceStatus`.
Every runtime this vocabulary can currently describe is user-attached, so
a second member would be a label no code path can produce, which every
later maintainer reads as meaningful state. Adding one is a single
``ALTER TYPE``; un-teaching a misunderstood label is not.

runtime_privilege_mode.description: Requested runtime privilege mode. Send privileged to enable sudo/privileged runtime support; send standard to disable; omit to leave unchanged. Privileged mode is enterprise-only and forces the bot runtime class to Kata.

BotUpdate.description:
Request to update bot metadata (avatar, tier).

Omitted fields are left unchanged. Send null to clear nullable fields.

For config changes, use PATCH /{bot_slug}/config instead.

executable_path.title: Executable Path
executable_path.description: Absolute path to the Chromium-compatible browser binary OpenClaw should launch. Defaults to the wrapper ``provision.sh`` installs, which resolves the Playwright-bundled chromium in the tools component at exec time (so the path survives tools-component hot-upgrades). Set to ``None`` to fall back to OpenClaw's PATH-based discovery (Chrome/Brave/Edge/Chromium/Chrome Canary).

no_sandbox.title: No Sandbox
no_sandbox.description: Add ``--no-sandbox`` to Chromium's launch args. Required for non-root container deployments where Chromium's setuid + namespace sandboxes can't initialise. Default ``True`` because every Botyard bot pod runs non-root.

headless.title: Headless
headless.description: Force headless launch. Required for our pods, which have no ``DISPLAY`` (no X server, no Wayland compositor). When ``executable_path`` is set, OpenClaw's plugin doesn't auto-infer headless from the binary name — it must be told explicitly via this flag. Default ``True`` because every Botyard bot pod is a server environment with no display.

BrowserConfig.title: BrowserConfig
BrowserConfig.description:
OpenClaw browser plugin configuration.

The browser plugin (powering ``mcp__openclaw__browser_*`` tools)
can launch a local Chromium-based browser or attach to a remote
CDP endpoint. Botyard ships the binary in the curated tools
component (``/components/tools/<ver>/playwright-browsers/``) and
installs a wrapper script at ``/home/openclaw/bin/chromium`` via
``bot/scripts/provision.sh``. The wrapper resolves the bundled
``chromium-<rev>/chrome-linux/chrome`` at exec time so the path
survives tools-component hot-upgrades that aren't coordinated with
a bridge redeploy (the curated tools layer can ship a different
chromium revision without rerunning provision). Pointing
``executable_path`` at the wrapper bypasses OpenClaw's discovery
cascade (Chrome → Brave → Edge → Chromium → Chrome Canary on PATH)
and avoids the bundled-revision-mismatch problem (OpenClaw vendors
a specific ``playwright-core`` whose ``browsers.json`` revision
may not match the nixpkgs-shipped one — explicit ``executable_path``
skips that revision check).

``no_sandbox=True`` is the right default for our deployment: every
bot pod is non-root with no ``CAP_SYS_ADMIN``, so Chromium's
sandbox can't initialise. Without ``--no-sandbox`` the browser
fails to start with a confusing error.

CliWatchdogConfig.title: CliWatchdogConfig
CliWatchdogConfig.description:
OpenClaw CLI watchdog overrides for the ``claude-cli`` backend.

Applied to ``cliBackends.claude-cli.reliability.watchdog`` by the
serializer. Both ``fresh`` (first turn of a session) and ``resume``
(every subsequent turn) profiles can be overridden independently.

Why we ship non-empty defaults: the upstream openclaw resume defaults
(``minMs=60_000``, ``maxMs=180_000``) are too tight for real bash
workloads — a single SQL query against a large table easily produces
no stdout for >3 minutes, and the watchdog kills the CLI mid-turn.
Our default raises ``maxMs`` to 15 min (900 s) so silent-but-progressing
tool calls don't get killed, while still detecting genuinely-stuck CLIs.

no_output_timeout_ms.title: No Output Timeout Ms
no_output_timeout_ms.description: Explicit no-output timeout in ms. When set, overrides the ratio/min/max computation. Capped by OpenClaw at ``timeoutMs - 1s``.

no_output_timeout_ratio.title: No Output Timeout Ratio
no_output_timeout_ratio.description: Fraction of the total turn ``timeoutMs`` used when ``no_output_timeout_ms`` is unset. Clamped to ``[0.05, 0.95]`` by OpenClaw.

min_ms.title: Min Ms
min_ms.description: Lower bound on the resolved no-output timeout (ms).

max_ms.title: Max Ms
max_ms.description: Upper bound on the resolved no-output timeout (ms).

CliWatchdogProfile.title: CliWatchdogProfile
CliWatchdogProfile.description:
One side of OpenClaw's CLI watchdog (fresh vs. resume turns).

Mirrors OpenClaw's per-turn-type watchdog override shape, applied to the
``cliBackends.<id>.reliability.watchdog.{fresh,resume}`` block by the
serializer.

OpenClaw resolves the per-turn no-output timeout via, roughly::

    noOutputTimeoutMs ?? clamp(timeoutMs * noOutputTimeoutRatio, minMs, maxMs)

capped by ``timeoutMs - 1s``. The upstream defaults (see
``cli-watchdog-defaults`` in the openclaw dist) put the **resume** cap at
180 s — that's the watchdog that fires when a single Bash tool call runs
silently for > 3 minutes (e.g. a Snowflake ``SELECT`` against a large
table) and SIGKILLs the whole CLI session mid-turn. Raising the cap is
the platform-level fix; bots can still override per-bot.

reserve_tokens.title: Reserve Tokens
reserve_tokens.description: Token headroom reserved for reply generation and tool output after compaction. Derived per-model from the context window (``max(round(cw * 0.16), 16000)``); None omits the key so OpenClaw uses its built-in (16384). Omitted for native-compaction backends.

reserve_tokens_floor.title: Reserve Tokens Floor
reserve_tokens_floor.description: Minimum floor enforced for reserve_tokens in compaction paths (0 disables the floor guard). None omits the key.

mid_turn_precheck.title: Mid Turn Precheck
mid_turn_precheck.description: Run a context-pressure precheck after each tool result so a single large result triggers compaction mid-turn instead of overflowing the next model call. OpenClaw's built-in is off. None omits the key.

truncate_after_compaction.title: Truncate After Compaction
truncate_after_compaction.description: Rotate the active session transcript to a compacted successor after compaction so future turns load only the summary plus tail, bounding growth. OpenClaw's built-in is off. None omits the key.

max_active_transcript_bytes.title: Max Active Transcript Bytes
max_active_transcript_bytes.description: Trigger proactive local compaction when the active transcript reaches this byte size, independent of (unreliable) token estimates. Derived per-model as ``context_window * 40`` (~40 bytes/token for tool-heavy bots). None omits the key.

timeout_seconds.title: Timeout Seconds
timeout_seconds.description: Maximum wall-clock seconds allowed for one local compaction operation. Botyard defaults to 10 minutes because large history summaries can legitimately exceed OpenClaw's shorter runtime default. Global (not per-model); always emitted.

CompactionConfig.title: CompactionConfig
CompactionConfig.description:
Context-compaction safeguards serialized into the openclaw config.

Defaults harden bots against the overflow -> failed-compaction ->
stuck-session-write-lock trap (upstream openclaw #699 / #70334). Only
serializers whose schema exposes these keys emit them (v2026.6.1+);
older versions ignore the fields.

The token-budget knobs are ``| None`` so the builder can OMIT them for a bot
whose primary model is routed through a backend that owns native compaction
(claude-cli, Codex harness), where they are inert. The concrete field
defaults reproduce the historical 200k-window derivation, so a config built
without the credential-driven resolution still emits sane safeguards.
``timeout_seconds`` stays a non-optional global (a compaction-operation
wall-clock cap, not a per-model attribute) and is always emitted.

reserve_tokens.title: Reserve Tokens
reserve_tokens.description: Reply/tool headroom tokens reserved after compaction.

mid_turn_precheck.title: Mid Turn Precheck
mid_turn_precheck.description: Run a tool-loop context precheck before the next model call.

truncate_after_compaction.title: Truncate After Compaction
truncate_after_compaction.description: Rotate the active transcript to a compacted successor.

max_active_transcript_bytes.title: Max Active Transcript Bytes
max_active_transcript_bytes.description: Byte size that triggers proactive local compaction.

timeout_seconds.title: Timeout Seconds
timeout_seconds.description: Maximum seconds allowed for one compaction operation.

Compaction parts contain an opaque or readable summary of prior messages,
produced by provider-specific compaction mechanisms. They must be round-tripped
back to the same provider in subsequent requests.

For Anthropic, `content` contains a readable text summary.
For OpenAI, `content` is `None` and the encrypted data is stored in `provider_details`.

tool_result_max_chars.title: Tool Result Max Chars
tool_result_max_chars.description: Ceiling for a single live tool result before truncation, in chars. Botyard pins OpenClaw's small-context default (16000, ~4k tokens) for every model instead of letting the >=200k-token auto cap (64000) apply, which is what lets a single 30-76 KB MCP response occupy the window. The value can only lower the effective cap — OpenClaw takes ``min(floor(contextWindow * 0.3) * 4, cap)`` — and truncation is explicit (a truncation notice is appended, minimum 2000 chars kept). None omits the key so OpenClaw uses its auto cap.

memory_get_max_chars.title: Memory Get Max Chars

memory_get_default_lines.title: Memory Get Default Lines

post_compaction_max_chars.title: Post Compaction Max Chars
post_compaction_max_chars.description: Max chars retained from AGENTS.md during post-compaction context refresh injection. None omits the key so OpenClaw uses its built-in default.

ContextLimitsConfig.title: ContextLimitsConfig
ContextLimitsConfig.description:
Per-agent context budget ceilings serialized into the openclaw config.

The load-bearing knob is :attr:`tool_result_max_chars`. OpenClaw caps a
single *live* tool result at ``min(floor(contextWindow * 0.3) * 4, cap)``
chars (``resolveLiveToolResultMaxChars`` /
``calculateMaxToolResultCharsWithCap``), where ``cap`` is this config value
when set and otherwise an auto cap derived from the model's context window:
16k chars under 100k tokens, 32k at >=100k, **64k at >=200k**. Every Botyard
bot on a modern model therefore lands in the 64k bucket, so a single tool
result may legally consume ~16k tokens of context.

That auto cap is the mechanism behind the chronic context overflows: measured
botyard-mcp responses on a real bot (13-minute window, ~600 KB total) were
``search_conversation_history`` 76 KB, ``memory_search`` 36 KB, ``get_task``
31 KB, ``github_list_prs`` 31 KB, ``search_tasks`` 29 KB, ``list_my_tasks``
22 KB — i.e. all but one pass the 64k cap untouched, and a handful of them
fill the window. Sessions were observed overflowing at ~258k compaction
tokens with only 47-72 messages.

Unlike :class:`ContextPruningConfig` this does not depend on prompt-cache
eligibility — ``resolveAgentContextLimits`` takes no provider or auth input,
and the persistence write path is ungated (it even falls back to 16000
rather than "unbounded" when the context window is unknown). So on the
**embedded (pi) runner** it applies to every bot whatever model backs it.

Two scope limits worth knowing before relying on it:

* On **claude-cli** bots it does not bound the CLI's context at all. Claude
  Code's tool results never reach OpenClaw's persistence write path; the cap
  only feeds ``shouldPreemptivelyCompactBeforePrompt``'s size estimate.
* The mid-turn guard consumer reads it via ``midTurnPrecheckOptions``, so
  that particular path is live only because Botyard sets
  ``compaction.mid_turn_precheck=True``. The write-time cap itself is
  unconditional.

mode.title: Mode
mode.description: ``cache-ttl`` prunes old tool results once the prompt cache TTL has elapsed; ``off`` disables pruning. None omits the key, which lets OpenClaw's Anthropic auto-default (``cache-ttl`` + 1h TTL) apply.

ttl.title: Ttl
ttl.description: How long after the last prompt-cache touch before pruning may run. Defaults to None (key omitted) so OpenClaw's own value applies — its built-in is 5m and ``applyAnthropicConfigDefaults`` installs 1h for Anthropic auth, paired with a 1h heartbeat that keeps an extended cache warm. Lowering it prunes into a still-warm cache and busts it; see the class docstring before overriding.

min_prunable_tool_chars.title: Min Prunable Tool Chars
min_prunable_tool_chars.description: Minimum total chars across prunable tool results before the hard-clear pass runs (soft-trim is not gated by it). The gate is summed over **post-soft-trim** sizes, so a result saturated at ``tool_result_max_chars`` has already been cut to ~3.1k chars (``softTrim`` head 1500 + tail 1500 + notice) by the time it counts: OpenClaw's built-in 50000 needs ~16 such results, and this 32000 needs ~10. A modest loosening, not the two-result trigger it looks like — the knob that actually decides how hard pruning bites is ``softTrim.maxChars``, which Botyard does not currently override. None omits the key.

keep_last_assistants.title: Keep Last Assistants
keep_last_assistants.description: Number of trailing assistant turns kept unpruned. None omits the key so OpenClaw uses its built-in (3).

ContextPruningConfig.title: ContextPruningConfig
ContextPruningConfig.description:
Cache-TTL pruning of *old tool results* out of the in-memory context.

Complements compaction rather than duplicating it. Compaction summarises
*conversation* messages and explicitly refuses to run when there are none
("[compaction] skipping — no real conversation messages"), which is why a
second overflow inside one turn is unrecoverable: after the first compaction
rotates the transcript, the window refills with tool output that compaction
will not touch. Pruning is the only mechanism that reclaims that space —
it soft-trims oversized old tool results (head+tail with a ``...`` marker)
and hard-clears the rest to a placeholder, in memory only; the on-disk
transcript is never rewritten.

**Known limitation — this does not reach every bot.** OpenClaw registers the
pruning extension only in the embedded (``pi``) agent runner, and only when
``isCacheTtlEligibleProvider`` holds: provider ``anthropic`` /
``anthropic-vertex``, an Anthropic model on Bedrock, ``modelApi ==
anthropic-messages``, or Gemini 2.5/3 on ``google-generative-ai``. A bot
whose primary is an OpenAI-family model routed through the Botyard proxy is
*not* eligible and gets nothing from this block — for those bots
:class:`ContextLimitsConfig` is the whole fix. Emitting it anyway is
deliberate: it is inert where ineligible, and where eligible it turns
pruning on for providers nothing auto-configures (Gemini).

**``ttl`` is deliberately not set here.** It is a prompt-cache *coherence*
knob, not a responsiveness one: pruning rewrites the prompt prefix, so the
TTL exists to hold pruning back until the provider's prompt cache has
lapsed anyway, at which point the re-cache is free. OpenClaw's Anthropic
auto-config is a matched set — ``ttl: 1h`` alongside a 1h heartbeat that
deliberately keeps an extended cache warm — and overriding the TTL alone
would prune into that warm cache and bust it, precisely when it is most
expensive (pruning only engages once the context is >=30% full). Since this
block is inert on the OpenAI-family bots that were actually overflowing,
any TTL we pinned would apply *only* to bots that were not failing. Leave it
to OpenClaw unless there is a measured cache-cost/context-pressure tradeoff
to act on.

ConversationSource.title: ConversationSource
ConversationSource.description:
How a conversation entered the platform.

``web_chat`` is the default for app/chat-proxy origin (existing
behaviour). Email sources are retained for compatibility with historical
channel plans. Current Bot Email is captured by the Resend webhook in the
API; see ``docs/design/2026-07-27-email-service-boundaries.md``.

``scheduler`` marks a conversation auto-created to host an externalized
schedule's wakes (EPIC #493). These are automation threads, not
user-initiated chats, so conversation-listing surfaces hide them (see
``conversation_visibility_predicate``); the bot still reaches them
directly via the wake's ``conversation_id``.

``ms_teams`` marks conversations created by the Teams dispatcher on first
inbound contact.

assertion.title: Assertion
assertion.description: A compact JWS (private_key_jwt shape), alg ES256, signed by the device's long-lived P-256 private key. 'kid' is the device id; 'aud' is 'botyard:device-assertion'; 'exp' - 'iat' may not exceed 120 seconds, and the 'jti' may be exchanged exactly once

DeviceAssertionExchangeRequest.title: DeviceAssertionExchangeRequest
DeviceAssertionExchangeRequest.description:
A device presenting proof that it holds its registered private key.

The assertion is the entire request. There is no device id, bot id or
anything else alongside it, deliberately: every identity claim is inside
the signed blob, so nothing here can assert an identity the signature does
not cover.

session_token.title: Session Token
session_token.description: Opaque session token, returned once. Not a JWT on purpose: a self-contained token would necessarily stay valid until it expired, which is the expiry-based validity this design removed

runtime_id.title: Runtime Id
runtime_id.description: The runtime this session authenticates. Minted control-plane side and stable across reconnects; this is the protocol's runtime_id

device_id.title: Device Id
device_id.description: Device whose key bought this session

gateway_url.title: Gateway Url
gateway_url.description: Origin of the runtime gateway this session should be used against, e.g. 'wss://runtime.botyard.io'. An ORIGIN, not a full URL: the daemon appends the runtime route itself, so an operator cannot point a fleet at the wrong path. Returned on every exchange rather than configured on the device, so a hostname change reaches the fleet on its next assertion exchange — which is not the same as its next reconnect, because a live session handle is reused for its lifetime even across a dropped socket

spiffe_id.title: Spiffe Id
spiffe_id.description: SPIFFE-shaped identity this session asserts. Botyard-issued and SPIFFE-shaped; it is not an SVID and no SPIRE trust domain backs it

expires_at.title: Expires At
expires_at.description: When this session stops being reusable. Bounds session reuse, NOT device validity

trust_tier.description: Deployment shape recorded on the runtime record. Non-security-bearing: no authorization decision branches on it

effect_coverage.description: How much of this runtime's externally visible effect surface Botyard mediates. 'partial' for v0. A governance claim, not a negotiated capability — it is persisted on the runtime record and is deliberately absent from the protocol handshake

DeviceAssertionExchangeResponse.title: DeviceAssertionExchangeResponse
DeviceAssertionExchangeResponse.description:
A short-lived session, bought by one assertion.

``session_token`` is returned exactly once and is never recoverable — only
its hash is stored.

*** THE TOKEN IS NOT A BEARER CAPABILITY AND ITS EXPIRY IS NOT THE
REVOCATION MECHANISM. *** Every use of it re-reads the device registry, so
a revoked device is denied on its next call whatever ``expires_at`` says.
``expires_at`` bounds how long a session may be reused; it says nothing
about how long a revoked device keeps working, which is "not at all".

``gateway_url`` is returned here rather than configured on the device. The
exchange is a live registry read, so sourcing the URL from it makes "holds
a gateway URL" imply "is a currently-valid device" — a stronger property
than enrollment can give, since enrollment only evidences a past event.

DeviceEnrollmentResponse.title: DeviceEnrollmentResponse
DeviceEnrollmentResponse.description:
A device this machine is, as of this call.

Carries only what the daemon needs to know which bot it now is. No
session, assertion or SVID is issued here — that belongs to the gateway,
and the device credential buys only the right to *ask* for one.

*** EVERY FIELD HERE CAME FROM THE DEVICE REGISTRY DURING THIS REQUEST.
*** That is the purpose of the response rather than a remark about it: an
installer may report success on what this call returned, and never on what
it found lying in ``~/.botyard``. A machine reading its own state file
cannot tell which bot that file belongs to *today*, nor whether the device
it names has since been revoked — and one that decided it could reported a
healthy install while holding revoked credentials for an unrelated bot.

This identifier can be provided to the model in a message to allow it to refer to this file in a tool call argument,

It's also included in inline-text delimiters for providers that require inlining text documents, so the model can
distinguish multiple files.

How an org proved it owns a provider tenant.

``CLAIM_CODE`` is a secret the org issued and a user pasted into the chat.
``ADMIN_CONSENT`` is a verified tenant id from an Entra consent callback —
stronger, and the only form that can be trusted without a human relaying it.
A tenant id typed into a form is neither, and is deliberately not a member.

ExternalChatTenantPatch.title: ExternalChatTenantPatch
ExternalChatTenantPatch.description:
Change which bot answers, or unlink the tenant.

Omitted means unchanged, so a caller flipping ``is_active`` does not have to
restate the default bot and risk clearing it.

``UNSET`` rather than ``None`` as the "omitted" marker, because the two
fields disagree about what null means and collapsing them is a real bug:
null on ``default_bot_id`` legitimately clears the default, whereas null on
``is_active`` is meaningless and must not be coerced into ``False`` — that
would turn a malformed request into a silent unlink. Leaving ``None`` out of
``is_active``'s union makes that unrepresentable rather than merely
unlikely; an explicit null is a 422.

IntegrationTokenRequest.title: IntegrationTokenRequest
IntegrationTokenRequest.description:
Body for POST /v1/integrations/token.

There is no ``credential_id`` field, and there never should be. The
credential is derived server-side from the caller's verified identity, so asking for another instance's credential is not a request the
server refuses — it is a request that cannot be expressed.

``provider`` only ever *narrows* within what the caller already holds, and
is needed only when a principal is granted credentials for more than one
provider (``design.md`` §3.3). With a single grant the body is empty.

expires_at.title: Expires At
expires_at.description: When the access token expires, if the provider reported an expiry. Absent means the provider issued no expiry, not that it never expires.

IntegrationTokenResponse.title: IntegrationTokenResponse
IntegrationTokenResponse.description:
The vended credential material — and deliberately nothing else.

No refresh token, no client secret, no vault path. A pod receives a
short-lived bearer and nothing with which to mint another, which is what
makes the platform the single writer of the refresh token by construction
rather than by convention (``design.md`` §4.2).

LlmChainEntry.title: LlmChainEntry
LlmChainEntry.description:
One credential link, in the bot's routing order — stored losslessly.

This is the **authoritative** record of a bot's LLM routing.
``primary``/``fallbacks``/``allowed_models``/``providers`` are derived from
it by :func:`derive_routing`; none of them is stored.

Why it has to live here rather than in ``bot_credential_links``: that table
is keyed ``(bot_id, scope, ordinal)`` and apply is a destructive
scope-replace, so ordinal — the very thing a reorder changes — is rewritten
and a removed entry's row simply vanishes. There is no stable per-entry
identity to hang a ``current_*`` column on, which is why credentials alone
can never answer "what was the chain before this change?". Storing the
chain in the config puts it on the same desired/reconciled footing as every
other stateful thing on the bot.

Why it can't be recovered from the derived fields either: an HTTP link
projects to ``ModelRef(provider="botyard", model=<id>)``, which carries no
credential identity, and :func:`derive_routing` collapses CLI entries that
share a ref, so the derived ref count is not the chain length. The
projection is lossy in that direction — which is exactly why the chain
itself must not be. One entry per eligible credential link, always; the
collapse happens at projection time and never in storage.

``routed_model`` is None for CLI-backed links — they are delivered through
``agents.defaults.cliBackends``, not ``models.providers``. Carrying the
resolved model here (rather than re-reading the credential preset) is what
keeps derivation a **pure, synchronous** function: the serializer has no
database session, so anything the wire format needs must already be in the
config.

model it carries is serializer input — context windows, token budgets,
compaction knobs — and nothing in the UI reads it. Projecting instead of
echoing the stored entry keeps a bot detail response from growing by a
kilobyte per linked credential.

MaintenancePolicyConfig.description:
Editable, persisted maintenance policy (per-org default).

Stored as JSONB on ``organizations.maintenance_policy`` (``None`` = no
configured policy, fall back to the hard-coded defaults). Distinct from
:class:`MaintenanceRestartPolicy`, which is the *resolved per-restart
snapshot* the engine consumes: :func:`resolve_restart_policy` turns this
config plus the restart's urgency into that snapshot.

``enabled=False`` opts the org out of workload-aware gating entirely —
regular restarts then apply immediately (today's blunt behaviour) instead
of waiting for idle/drain, while critical restarts are always immediate
regardless of this flag.

MaintenanceRestartForceAppliedContent.title: MaintenanceRestartForceAppliedContent
MaintenanceRestartForceAppliedContent.description:
Typed content for an operator force-applying a pending maintenance restart.

Emitted when a platform admin invokes the "apply pending maintenance restart
now" fleet action, overriding the maintenance-window gate so a deferred /
parked restart lands immediately instead of waiting for the org's window.
``immediate`` records whether the operator chose to hard-kill this tick
(interrupting any active turn) versus a graceful drain; ``previous_phase`` is
the maintenance phase the restart was parked in before the override (e.g.
``deferred``); ``applied`` is whether the pod recreate landed within the
synchronous call (a graceful override on a still-busy bot may report ``False``
and finish draining on a later reconcile tick).

MaintenanceRestartMessageError.description:
A turn cut short because the bot was restarted for maintenance.

Not a failure of the bot or the provider: the runtime was deliberately
hard-killed mid-turn (a maintenance evict), so the turn was abandoned. The
request was never answered and is safe to send again, which is why clients
render this neutrally — "restarting, send it again" — rather than as an
error the user should worry about.

McpCredentialDestinationAcknowledgedCont.title: McpCredentialDestinationAcknowledgedContent
McpCredentialDestinationAcknowledgedCont.description:
Typed content for accepting a new destination for an org's secrets.

A managed-remote MCP row with Runtime Vault-backed ``secret_headers`` has
its secrets resolved server-side into every outbound request, so whoever
owns ``endpoint_url`` owns where they land. Nominating that host is
permitted — the operator is the org owner, and the vault is theirs — but
it is not permitted *quietly*, which is what this event is for.

``acknowledged_host`` is what the caller explicitly accepted, recorded
separately from ``new_host`` even though the service refuses unless they
match: the record should show the acceptance as the caller expressed it,
not merely the outcome the server derived.

``secret_key_paths`` are vault *references*, never values — the same
strings already stored on the row. The values are resolved at dial time
and appear nowhere in the database, the logs, or here.

McpPodHostMode.title: McpPodHostMode
McpPodHostMode.description:
How Botyard sets the HTTP ``Host`` when connecting to an in-cluster MCP pod.

This is a fixed property of the server's HTTP framework, declared as
configuration (like ``port``) rather than discovered at runtime:

* ``natural`` — send the pod's in-cluster Service FQDN as ``Host`` (httpx's
  default). Correct for the MCP Python SDK / uvx, Node/npx, and every
  first-party ``ghcr.io/botyard-ai/*`` wrapper image. The default.
* ``pod_localhost`` — send ``Host: localhost:<port>``. Required by servers
  that enforce DNS-rebinding host allowlists (``mark3labs/mcp-go``, e.g.
  ``grafana/mcp-grafana``), which reject the Service FQDN with
  ``403 forbidden: host not allowed``. Sending it to a server that does not
  want it (Python SDK) instead breaks the handshake with ``Session
  terminated`` (the server's ``307`` echoes the forged Host back to the
  client's own localhost).

Only meaningful for ``runtime_kind=container_image``; ignored for
``managed_remote`` (the vendor host is always preserved).

included.title: Included
included.description: Portion of ``quantity`` within the included baseline, when the series carries a per-bucket split (resource-overage meters). The overage portion is ``quantity - included``. Null for count meters, whose included threshold is a flat plan scalar (``OrgUsageMeter.included_units``) the client applies as a cap instead.

MeterHistoryPoint.description: One bucket in a meter history series.

MeterHistorySeries.description:
Per-meter usage history returned by ``GET /v1/orgs/{org_id}/usage/history``.

``points`` is empty when the meter has no events for the org in the
requested window — a fresh org or a brand-new meter both render as
a flat-zero chart without any special-casing on the FE.

MeterInfo.title: MeterInfo
MeterInfo.description: A meter definition from the billing provider.

MeterKey.title: MeterKey
MeterKey.description:
Registry meter slugs — every countable unit a plan can gate on.

All meters are metered (Polar ``metered_unit`` + optional
``meter_credit`` benefit for included units). An entry here means the
slug is recognized by the codebase; an entry in
``scripts/billing/registry.py::METER_DEFINITIONS`` wires it to the
provider.

The ``*_COUNT`` meters are AVG-over-daily-snapshots counts (bots, seats,
MCP servers). The ``*_OVERAGE`` meters bill the same way — AVG over daily
snapshots — but of the day's time-average net resource-overage from the
allocation ledger (vCore for CPU, GiB for memory/storage), priced at an
integer €/unit-month rate (the "GB-Month" convention, calendar-independent).
Each meters one billable :class:`MeteredResource` line-item independently —
the included baseline is subtracted per-interval in the collector, so the
snapshot carries net overage (Polar prices the averaged units; no
meter-credit benefit). ``memory_request`` and ``gpu`` are recorded in the
ledger but not metered to the provider yet.

MeteredResource.title: MeteredResource
MeteredResource.description:
A billable resource line-item the allocation ledger meters independently.

The ledger is long: one interval row per ``(consumer, metered_resource)``.
CPU and memory split into a reserved floor (``*_request``) and a burstable
ceiling (``*_limit``) because they are priced on both dimensions; storage and
gpu are single-dimension (fully reserved). New line-items are added by
extending this enum + a one-time migration — never by widening the table.

NativeToolCallPart.title: NativeToolCallPart
NativeToolCallPart.description:
A tool call to a native tool.

For native tools with a stable cross-provider shape (currently `tool_search`), this base
class can be promoted to a typed subclass with a narrowed `args` `TypedDict`. See
[`NativeToolSearchCallPart`][pydantic_ai.messages.NativeToolSearchCallPart] for the
canonical example.

Adding a typed subclass for a future native tool (see `pydantic_ai._tool_search` for
a worked example):

1. Add a sibling `pydantic_ai/_<name>.py` module that defines the cross-provider
   `TypedDict`s, the `NativeToolCallPart` / `NativeToolReturnPart` subclasses,
   and registers their narrowers into `_NATIVE_CALL_NARROWERS` /
   `_NATIVE_RETURN_NARROWERS` keyed by `tool_kind`. Subclass overrides
   `tool_kind: Literal['<emitter>']` to match the emitting
   [`AbstractNativeTool.kind`][pydantic_ai.native_tools.AbstractNativeTool.kind],
   and shadows `args` / `content` with a narrower type.
2. Late-import the new module from this file (alongside the existing tool-search
   import) so registration runs whenever `pydantic_ai.messages` is imported.
3. Add the subclass to `ModelResponsePart`'s discriminated union and to
   `_model_response_part_discriminator` so Pydantic deserialization auto-promotes
   on `model_validate` / `model_validate_json`.

Dispatch is by `tool_kind`, not `tool_name`. This protects users whose tools happen to
share a name with one of ours from accidentally getting their parts promoted (and
failing shape validation against the typed `args`/`content`).

The `provider_details` field carries genuinely non-portable provider extras
(e.g. Anthropic's `strategy: 'bm25' | 'regex'` for tool search). Promote a field
to a typed slot in `args` / `content` only when at least two of OpenAI, Anthropic,
and Google support it (cf. [issue #3885](https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic-ai/issues/3885)).

MCP server tools land here with `tool_kind='mcp_server'` (label stays in
`tool_name='mcp_server:<label>'`); typed-subclass work for MCP is tracked by
[issue #3561](https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic-ai/issues/3561).

with a narrowed `content` `TypedDict`. See `NativeToolCallPart` for the pattern.

NativeToolSearchCallPart-Input.title: NativeToolSearchCallPart
NativeToolSearchCallPart-Input.description:
Typed view of a [`NativeToolCallPart`][pydantic_ai.messages.NativeToolCallPart] for tool search.

Used on the native server-side tool-search path (Anthropic BM25/regex, OpenAI
Responses) where the provider executes the search and emits a native result.
The local-fallback path uses
[`ToolSearchCallPart`][pydantic_ai.messages.ToolSearchCallPart] instead.

To detect a tool-search part regardless of execution path (native server-side
vs. local fallback), check `part.tool_kind == 'tool-search'` — this works
across both call/return and both server/local variants.

Shadows `args` with a narrower type. The `str` variant covers the
streaming / partial-args case before parsing completes; once parsed,
`args` is a [`ToolSearchArgs`][pydantic_ai.messages.ToolSearchArgs]
`TypedDict`.

The local-fallback path uses

To detect a tool-search part regardless of execution path (native server-side

tool_search.description: Tool Search. Defers tool schemas behind a search surface instead of inlining all of them in every prompt. Auto by default; owners can opt out per bot. OpenClawBotConfig.title: OpenClawBotConfig
OpenClawBotConfig.description:
Platform-level bot config — the input to version-specific serialization.

Only includes fields that are platform-specific or that we explicitly
control. OpenClaw fills defaults for everything else at load time.

Stored as JSONB in bots.desired_config. The ``bot_type`` field acts as
the discriminator for a future union of bot-type configs.

``extra="ignore"`` ensures old data with removed fields doesn't break
on read (schema evolution safety).
